summary:
Mississippi's own statutes, not the national framework, set the terms a trans visitor meets inside the state. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records that Mississippi enacted bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity in 2024 and 2025, and that state statute defines sex by birth. The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update places Mississippi in its "Worst Laws Passed" category, among states the assessment describes as having legislatively erased transgender people; the grading derives from a five-year legislation-tracking methodology with a scoring rubric.

Facilities rules bite first in schools. A law signed 13 May 2024 and effective immediately requires individuals in public schools to use bathrooms consistent with sex "determined solely by birth." In 2024 a Harrison County dress code requiring clothing to match sex assigned at birth led to a transgender girl being threatened with in-school suspension for wearing a dress to a regional band event. Two earlier bills, the SAFER Act restricting transgender people's use of public bathrooms, locker rooms and public university dormitories, and the Women's Bill of Rights codifying a binary definition of sex at birth, died on 29 April 2024 when House and Senate negotiators failed to agree on compromise versions; the 2024 and 2025 enactments followed that failure.

Identity documents are closed at state level. The Vital Records office issues an amended birth certificate with a new name and gender marker on a certified court order, a medical statement attesting to gender reassignment, and a fee, but the amended certificate lists both the updated and the original information. From 1 November 2021 to March 2026 a Gender Designation Form signed by a physician or psychotherapist allowed a driver's licence marker change; a March 2026 law prohibited markers not reflecting sex assigned at birth.

The state's highest court has ruled against recognition. On 17 April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court held 8-1 that a transgender teenager undergoing gender transition could not change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented. The majority opinion, written by Justice James D. Maxwell II, referred to the boy as a "minor female" and cited the 2023 REAP Act as Mississippi's express public policy against children receiving life-altering gender-transition assistance; a chancellor may grant a minor's name change only where it is clearly in the child's best interest. Minors may otherwise change names with parental consent.

Care access is restricted. The Regulate Experimental Adolescent Procedures (REAP) Act, signed 28 February 2023, bans gender-affirming care for people under 18. The University of Mississippi Medical Center's TEAM Clinic closed on 30 June 2023, leaving Spectrum: The Other Clinic in Hattiesburg, operating virtually, as the only LGBTQ+-specialising clinic in the state.

School sports participation is conditioned on proof of anatomy. SB 2536, signed 11 March 2021 and effective 1 July 2021, bars transgender students from school sports consistent with their gender identity and requires any athlete whose sex is disputed to provide a physician's statement verifying genitalia, DNA and hormone levels.

Anti-discrimination protection is absent at state level. Mississippi law provides no protection based on gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations, and the 1994 state hate-crime statute does not include gender identity.

The Religious Liberty Accommodations Act (HB 1523) protects individuals, religious organisations and some businesses that refuse services on the belief that gender is determined at birth by anatomy and genetics.

Violence against transgender people in Mississippi has drawn federal prosecution. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Mississippi reported that Joshua Brandon Vallum was sentenced to 49 years in federal prison for the bias-motivated murder of a transgender woman in Lucedale, committed after he learned his former girlfriend was transgender.

Marriage is recognised. Same-sex marriage has been recognised in Mississippi since the Supreme Court's ruling in Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, which overrode a 1996 executive order, a 1997 statutory ban and 2004 constitutional Amendment 1, approved by 86.01% of voters. Those bans remain unrepealed. A trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry, and the then Attorney General Jim Hood directed clerks to comply or face lawsuits on 29 June 2015 after initial resistance.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion in Mississippi is more supportive of protections than state law is. A 2019 PRRI poll found 68% of Mississippians favoured laws protecting gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people from discrimination in jobs, housing and public accommodations, with 23% opposed; by 2024 PRRI reported support for a statewide anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity at 67%. PRRI describes Mississippi as tending to show lower support for same-sex marriage and transgender rights than national averages, with the gap narrowing over time and pronounced generational differences, younger residents markedly more supportive than older ones.

Municipal law diverges from the state. Jackson, Clarksdale, Holly Springs and Magnolia ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations; Hattiesburg, Oxford and Starkville protect city employees only. Starkville hosted its first pride parade on 24 March 2018 after an initial permit denial, drawing approximately 3,000 participants and becoming the largest parade in the city's history.
localsOnly:
Residents convicted under Mississippi's sodomy statute before 2003 are still required to register as sex offenders under the 1995 registration law. The statute, originating in 1839 and carrying up to ten years' imprisonment, remains on the books but is unenforceable after Lawrence v. Texas (2003). Five residents sued in 2016 over the registration requirement, and $400,000 in taxpayer legal fees were reported in 2023.

Mississippi criminalises failure to disclose HIV-positive status to a sexual partner as a felony even where transmission does not occur; a 2024 Williams Institute report counted at least 43 arrests for HIV-related offences between 2004 and 2021.

A state measure prohibits inmate name changes, enacted after the Real You Act of 2022 died in committee.

Mississippi banned adoption and fostering by same-sex couples in 2000 and was the only state still enforcing such a ban by 2015; U.S. District Judge Daniel Porter Jordan III struck it down on 31 March 2016, with final effect on 2 May 2016 after no appeal, making Mississippi the last state to allow adoption by same-sex couples.
outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement data for Mississippi's 2024 and 2025 facilities bans is not sourced in the inventory; whether the 2025 enactment reaches adults in public buildings, or only schools, is unresolved.

The March 2026 law barring driver's licence markers that do not reflect sex assigned at birth is recorded by date and effect; its operative text, effective date and any exceptions are not sourced here.

No per-capita or comparative data on anti-transgender violence in Mississippi is available in the inventory; the Vallum prosecution is a single documented case and does not establish a rate.
